reference.source: Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics / Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive monosaccharide transport defect caused by SLC5A1 variants affecting the sodium/glucose cotransporter SGLT1
Presents in the neonatal period with severe watery osmotic diarrhoea beginning with the first milk feeds
Because SGLT1 also transports galactose, both glucose and galactose (and therefore lactose- and sucrose-containing feeds) provoke symptoms
The diarrhoea is osmotic and stops promptly on withdrawal of dietary glucose and galactose, with acidic stool and reducing substances
Fructose is absorbed by a different transporter and is tolerated, forming the basis of a fructose-based feed
Intermittent glucosuria may be present because SGLT1 contributes to renal monosaccharide handling
Lifelong avoidance of glucose and galactose with a fructose-based diet allows normal growth
reference.pathophysiology: Glucose-galactose malabsorption is an osmotic diarrhoea caused by defective apical monosaccharide uptake. Variants in SLC5A1 impair the sodium/glucose cotransporter SGLT1, which normally drives coupled absorption of glucose, galactose and sodium across the enterocyte brush border. When this transporter fails, glucose and galactose accumulate in the lumen along with sodium and water, producing a profuse osmotic diarrhoea. Because dietary lactose and sucrose are digested to these monosaccharides, all glucose- and galactose-containing feeds cause symptoms, whereas fructose, absorbed via GLUT5, is well tolerated.
additionalDifferentials: Congenital secretory diarrhoeas (chloride and sodium diarrhoea)
Microvillus inclusion disease and tufting enteropathy
additionalInvestigations: Stool pH and reducing substances demonstrating acidic sugar-containing stool
Faecal osmotic gap and response of diarrhoea to withdrawal of glucose and galactose
Glucose hydrogen breath test showing malabsorption
Molecular genetic testing for SLC5A1 variants
Urinalysis for intermittent glucosuria and monitoring of hydration and electrolytes
redFlags: Rapid severe dehydration in the neonate from high-volume osmotic diarrhoea
Failure to thrive if the offending sugars are not eliminated
Return of diarrhoea on dietary lapses containing glucose, galactose, lactose or sucrose
reference.prognosis: With a strict fructose-based diet free of glucose and galactose the prognosis is excellent and growth is normal; tolerance to small carbohydrate loads may improve modestly with age. Lifelong dietary vigilance is required.
pitfalls: Switching to a lactose-free but glucose-containing formula, which does not relieve symptoms
Confusing the disorder with lactase deficiency, missing the need to also exclude glucose and galactose
Overlooking hidden glucose and galactose sources in feeds, foods and medicines
references: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
management: Institute a strict glucose- and galactose-free diet, replacing lactose- and sucrose-containing feeds with a fructose-based formula that bypasses the defective SGLT1 transporter
Rehydrate and correct electrolyte and acid-base disturbance during the profuse osmotic diarrhoea, using oral rehydration or intravenous fluids in the acute neonatal presentation
Involve a paediatric dietitian to ensure nutritional adequacy and to guide cautious testing of carbohydrate tolerance, which may improve modestly with age
Monitor growth, hydration status and electrolytes, and confirm resolution of diarrhoea on withdrawal of dietary glucose and galactose
Offer genetic counselling for autosomal recessive inheritance, discussing recurrence risk and carrier testing for the family
Escalate to hospital assessment for any breakthrough diarrhoea causing dehydration or faltering growth
